channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today’s ranked reading list centers on silicon spin-qubit hardware and operational benchmarking: 2611.12850 proposes over-gate TiN stressors to enhance valley splitting in Si/SiGe wiggle-well dots, 2611.14114 offers a cloud-executed GHZ-fidelity benchmark that tests whether calibration data predict processor performance, and 2611.12217 maps how multi-dot configurations affect electron temperature and double-dot latching for initialization and readout. The skim-tier items broaden the context but sit further from current spin-qubit operation: 2611.13301 presents an MLIR-based fault-tolerant compiler, 2611.12779 a neutral-atom arbitrary two-qubit gate architecture, 2611.13371 silicon-spin qLDPC syndrome extraction with mobile ancillas, 2611.14422 a QRAM energetic-cost accounting method, and 2611.13796 an analog Rydberg-atom QAOA MaxCut study. No pay dirt today — 1 to read · 1 to skim.

item.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.description:
Read new result — Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N∗=27 and N∗=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N∗=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.

Grade 0.628 · 4.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing” · Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde, Uxue Ballarin Manso, Uxue Auzmendi, Iker Pastor, Pablo García Bringas, Ane Blázquez García, Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz

Figure

Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N∗ against total physical qubits Ntot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.

Asks

How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?

But

Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε=δ=0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.

Tools

QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs

Code. https://github.com/NQUIRE-Center/Cross-Platform-Benchmarking/tree/main/GHZ-State_Generation

Abstract

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array
item.description:
Skim new result — Constraining analog QAOA cost duration to γk≤1μs on 3D Rydberg arrays yields an annealing branch reaching approximation ratio Ra=0.959 at p=20, outperforming single-rounding Goemans-Williamson (Ra=0.948). Combining this cold-start annealing branch with a GNN warm start yields a portfolio reaching Ra=0.966.

Grade 0.389 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Accelerating HPC With Quantum Computing: It Is a Software Challenge Too” · Junxi Chen, I. I. Beterov

Figure

Approximation ratio Ra versus QAOA depth p for cold-start and warm-start protocols compared against the single-rounding Goemans-Williamson expectation. It shows the constrained annealing branch overtaking Goemans-Williamson near p=16 and the portfolio reaching Ra=0.966 at p=20.

Asks

Can an analog QAOA implemented on a three-dimensional Rydberg atom array solve the weighted MaxCut problem by encoding edge weights directly in interatomic couplings without gadgets?

Before

Without the duration constraint, layer-wise optimization of the analog sequence traps in a non-adiabatic basin saturating near Ra≈0.77. The single-rounding Goemans-Williamson classical algorithm achieves Ra=0.948 on these graphs.

But

Numerical emulation of 20 randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices. Under Aquila realistic processor noise (λ=1), optimal depth drops to p=3–5, performance falls below Goemans-Williamson (Ra=0.826), and optimal cut probability per shot is 16%.

Tools

3D Rydberg atom array (optical tweezers) · Analog QAOA · Bloqade.jl / Arnoldi trajectory emulator · Graph neural network (GNN) warm start · Aquila error model

Code. https://github.com/chenjunxi1997-cmd/QAOA-quantum-simulation-on-Bloqade.jl

Abstract

We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.
